title: Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Can Be Unreliable in Implicit-Influence Settings

bias_targets.methodology: Injecting irrelevant background details (e.g., ethical concerns, social proof, sunk cost, lifestyle cues, corporate reputation) as casual asides in prompts across binary choice, rating, and open-ended coding tasks to measure behavioral shifts.
Placing correct answers in few-shot examples at a consistent position (e.g., always option B) in hard multiple-choice QA tasks to measure whether the model covertly follows the positional pattern.

Adding demographic cues related to age (e.g., older candidates, Gen Z users) and gender as background details in binary preference elicitation and hiring rating tasks to observe changes in model outputs.
Including cues about class/profession or first-generation college student status in decision-making and essay grading prompts to measure shifts in model choices and numerical ratings.
Injecting details about learning disabilities into essay grading scenarios to measure statistically significant shifts in the model's assigned scores.
